topics.name: Crispus Attucks
topics.kicker: First to die in the Boston Massacre · Of African and Native American descent
topics.briefing: On the night of March 5, 1770, a tall sailor named Crispus Attucks stood with an angry crowd facing British soldiers on King Street in Boston. When the soldiers fired, he was the first of five colonists to die. A man of African and Native American descent who had probably escaped slavery twenty years earlier, he was later honored by abolitionists as the first martyr of the American Revolution.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1750, William Brown of Framingham placed an advertisement in the _Boston Gazette_ offering a reward for an enslaved man who had run away, describing him as 6 feet 2 inches tall. Historians believe that runaway was this man, who spent much of the next twenty years working as a sailor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man of African and Native American descent, the first person killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: A Boston newspaper reported that this man had been born in Framingham but had lately come from New Providence in the Bahamas, and that he was in town waiting for a ship to North Carolina. He made his living as a sailor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who was the first to die when British soldiers fired into a Boston crowd in 1770.

tossups.p: In his closing argument at the soldiers’ trial, John Adams said that this man had led the crowd that attacked them and was chiefly to blame for the bloodshed. Six of the eight soldiers were found not guilty, and two were convicted of manslaughter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this sailor, the first of five colonists killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: John Boyle O’Reilly’s poem for the 1888 unveiling of a monument on Boston Common calls this man “the first to defy, and the first to die.” That monument honors this man and the other four victims of the same night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man of African and Native American ancestry who died in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: In 1998, the U.S. Mint issued a silver dollar honoring Black patriots of the Revolutionary War, with this man’s portrait on the front. Abolitionists of the 1850s pointed to this man to argue that Black Americans had fought for liberty since the Revolution began.
tossups.r: He had been killed on King Street in 1770. For 10 points, name this first victim of the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: Oscar Robertson led an Indianapolis high school named for this man to Indiana state basketball championships in 1955 and 1956. That school had opened in 1927 as a segregated school for Black students.
tossups.r: Its namesake was a sailor of African and Native American descent. For 10 points, name this first person killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: In 1858, the Black abolitionist and historian William Cooper Nell began organizing yearly celebrations in Boston honoring this man on the anniversary of his death. Nell had earlier written about this man in a book about Black patriots of the American Revolution.
tossups.r: He died on March 5, 1770. For 10 points, name this man, the first person killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: This man and the sailor James Caldwell were not from Boston, so their bodies lay in Faneuil [“FAN-yul”] Hall before a shared funeral for the victims. Thousands of mourners joined the procession through the town.
tossups.r: He was buried with other victims in the Granary Burying Ground. For 10 points, name this sailor killed on King Street in 1770.

tossups.p: Below the picture in Paul Revere’s famous engraving, this man is named among the “unhappy Sufferers,” along with Samuel Gray, Samuel Maverick, James Caldwell, and Patrick Carr. Unlike Carr, who died days later, this man was killed on the spot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man, the first person to die in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: This man joined a crowd that gathered around Private Hugh White, a lone sentry outside the Custom House, after White struck a wigmaker’s apprentice with his musket. Captain Thomas Preston then marched seven soldiers to the sentry’s aid.
tossups.r: When the soldiers fired, this man was the first to fall. For 10 points, name this man of African and Native American descent.

tossups.p: Samuel Maverick, a 17-year-old apprentice, and Samuel Gray, a rope maker, were also killed in the event in which this man died. Patrick Carr, an Irish immigrant who was shot the same night, died nine days later.
tossups.r: This man was the first to die. For 10 points, name this sailor of African and Native American descent killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: This man was killed by soldiers of the 29th Regiment, one of the units sent to Boston in 1768 to protect customs officials collecting the Townshend duties. Colonists mocked those soldiers as “lobsterbacks” because of their red coats.
tossups.r: Captain Thomas Preston commanded the soldiers who fired. For 10 points, name this man, the first person killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: A circle of cobblestones near the Old State House marks the site of the shooting in which this man was killed, on what was then called King Street. He was part of a crowd that threw snowballs, ice, and insults at British soldiers that night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man of African and Native American descent who was the first person killed in the Boston Massacre.

tossups.p: On the day of this man’s funeral, most of Boston’s shops closed, and church bells tolled in the town and in neighboring towns such as Charlestown and Roxbury. He was laid to rest in one vault with three other victims.
tossups.r: He was one of five colonists killed when British soldiers fired on a crowd. For 10 points, name this man, the first to die in that 1770 event.

tossups.p: Three days before this man died, soldiers and rope makers brawled at John Gray’s ropewalk, a fight that began when a worker insulted a soldier who was looking for part-time work. Bad feelings between soldiers and workers spread across the town.
tossups.r: This man died when soldiers fired on a crowd on King Street. For 10 points, name this sailor, the first person killed in the Boston Massacre.

clues.t: The first person killed in the Boston Massacre, when British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston on March 5, 1770
A sailor of African and Native American descent (his Native ancestry is often given as Wampanoag or Natick)
Remembered as the first martyr of the American Revolution
Born around 1723 and enslaved in Framingham, Massachusetts; he escaped in 1750 and spent about 20 years as a sailor
Killed on King Street (now State Street) outside the Custom House; a circle of cobblestones near the Old State House marks the site
Killed by soldiers of the 29th Regiment, sent to Boston in 1768; their captain, Thomas Preston, was found not guilty
He was in a crowd that threw snowballs, ice, and insults at the soldiers
At the soldiers’ trial, John Adams argued that he had led the crowd and was chiefly to blame for the violence
Black abolitionist William Cooper Nell organized yearly celebrations in his honor, starting in 1858
Honored, with the other four victims, by a monument on Boston Common unveiled in 1888
In 1750, William Brown of Framingham advertised a reward for him in the _Boston Gazette_, describing him as 6 feet 2 inches tall
A 1770 newspaper said he had lately come from New Providence in the Bahamas and was waiting for a ship to North Carolina
Because he was not from Boston, his body lay in Faneuil Hall, with sailor James Caldwell’s, before the shared funeral
Buried in one vault with other victims in the Granary Burying Ground, near Paul Revere, Samuel Adams, and John Hancock
On the day of his funeral, Boston’s shops closed and bells tolled in Boston, Charlestown, and Roxbury
Named among the “unhappy Sufferers” below Paul Revere’s engraving of the massacre
The other victims: Samuel Gray (a rope maker), Samuel Maverick (a 17-year-old apprentice), James Caldwell, and Patrick Carr, who died nine days later
John Boyle O’Reilly’s poem for the 1888 monument calls him “the first to defy, and the first to die”
Pictured on a 1998 U.S. silver dollar honoring Black patriots of the Revolutionary War
Namesake of an Indianapolis high school where Oscar Robertson won state basketball titles in 1955 and 1956
The crowd he joined had gathered around sentry Hugh White, who had struck a wigmaker’s apprentice with his musket
Three days before his death, soldiers and rope makers brawled at John Gray’s ropewalk

trap.title: The man, not the massacre
trap.body: Almost every clue about Crispus Attucks is also a clue about the Boston Massacre: King Street, the Custom House, Captain Thomas Preston, John Adams’s defense of the soldiers, and Paul Revere’s engraving. If the question says “this man” or “this sailor,” the answer is Attucks, not the event. Other Black patriots of the Revolution come up too, like Peter Salem and Salem Poor, who fought at Bunker Hill, and James Armistead, who spied on the British before Yorktown.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this event” wants the Boston Massacre, while “this man” wants Attucks. Attucks clues are about dying on King Street in 1770; clues about fighting at Bunker Hill (1775) or spying for Lafayette (1781) point to someone else.

topics.name: Daniel Webster
topics.kicker: Massachusetts senator and orator · “Liberty and Union, now and forever”
topics.briefing: Daniel Webster was the most famous speechmaker of his age, a senator from Massachusetts who could hold a crowded Senate gallery spellbound for hours. In 1830 he closed his reply in a famous debate with the words “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!” He won landmark Supreme Court cases, served twice as secretary of state, and even stars in a short story where he out-argues the devil himself.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A debate over Samuel Foot’s resolution to limit sales of western land grew into this senator’s famous clash with Robert Hayne of South Carolina, while Vice President John C. Calhoun presided over the Senate. Hayne defended a state’s right to nullify federal laws.
tossups.r: This senator replied, “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!” For 10 points, name this Massachusetts orator.

tossups.p: John Greenleaf Whittier attacked this man in the poem “Ichabod,” whose title means “the glory has departed,” after this man spoke in favor of a stricter Fugitive Slave Act. Many abolitionists in his home state felt betrayed by that speech.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator who gave the Seventh of March speech in 1850.

tossups.p: This lawyer told the Supreme Court, “It is, sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it!” He won that case when John Marshall ruled that the college’s charter was a contract that New Hampshire could not change.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who won _Dartmouth College v. Woodward_ and later became a senator from Massachusetts.

tossups.p: This secretary of state and Lord Ashburton signed an 1842 treaty that settled the border between Maine and New Brunswick and set up joint naval patrols against the African slave trade. That treaty ended a dispute that had led to the bloodless “Aroostook War.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts statesman, the senator who said “Liberty and Union, now and forever.”

tossups.p: In the election of 1836, this man was one of several Whig candidates for president, but he carried only Massachusetts. With Henry Clay, he had helped found the Whig Party to oppose Andrew Jackson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this senator who formed the “Great Triumvirate” with Clay and John C. Calhoun.

tossups.p: On June 17, 1825, the 50th anniversary of a famous battle, this man gave the main speech at the laying of the Bunker Hill Monument’s cornerstone, with the Marquis de Lafayette looking on. He spoke again when the finished monument was dedicated in 1843.
tossups.r: He later served as secretary of state under three presidents. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator and orator.

tossups.p: This lawyer argued for the national bank in _McCulloch v. Maryland_ and for a steamboat operator in _Gibbons v. Ogden_, two cases won by his side before John Marshall’s Supreme Court. He also won a case protecting the charter of his old college.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer and Massachusetts senator who debated Robert Hayne in 1830.

tossups.p: In a short story by Stephen Vincent Benét [“beh-NAY”], this man defends the New Hampshire farmer Jabez Stone, who sold his soul to Mr. Scratch. This man wins the case before a jury of villains from American history, with Judge John Hathorne of the Salem witch trials presiding.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this real-life senator from Massachusetts, famous for his Seventh of March speech.

tossups.p: John F. Kennedy’s book _Profiles in Courage_ praises this senator for risking his career with a speech supporting the Compromise of 1850. In 1957, a Senate committee led by Kennedy named this man one of the five greatest senators in history.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator, part of the “Great Triumvirate” with Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun.

tossups.p: As a young Federalist congressman from New Hampshire, this man opposed the War of 1812 and gave a speech in 1814 against a plan to draft soldiers. He later moved to Boston and represented Massachusetts in both houses of Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this orator who said “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!”

tossups.p: This man was born in 1782 in Salisbury, New Hampshire, and graduated from Dartmouth College in 1801. A statue of this man represents New Hampshire in the U.S. Capitol’s National Statuary Hall collection.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who later represented Massachusetts in the Senate and served as secretary of state.

tossups.p: This man died in 1852 at his farm in Marshfield, Massachusetts, a few months after his fellow Whig Henry Clay. Two years earlier, Millard Fillmore had made him secretary of state for the second time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Whig orator who debated Robert Hayne of South Carolina in 1830.

tossups.p: George P. A. Healy’s enormous painting in Boston’s Faneuil [“FAN-yul”] Hall shows this senator standing to speak in a packed Senate chamber in January 1830. The speech it shows was a reply to a senator from South Carolina who defended nullification.
tossups.r: In that speech, he said, “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!” For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator.

tossups.p: William Henry Harrison chose this man as secretary of state in 1841, and this man was the only cabinet member to stay when the rest of the cabinet quit after John Tyler vetoed bills for a national bank.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts Whig, a member of the “Great Triumvirate” with Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun.

tossups.p: This senator began one speech, “I wish to speak today, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Northern man, but as an American.” In that speech, he angered many abolitionists by supporting a tougher law for returning people who had escaped slavery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this senator who gave the Seventh of March speech in support of the Compromise of 1850.

clues.t: Ended his “Second Reply to Hayne” (1830) with “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!”
The most famous orator of his age; represented Massachusetts in the House and the Senate
Formed the “Great Triumvirate” of senators with Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun
Seventh of March speech (1850): backed the Compromise of 1850, including a tougher Fugitive Slave Act
Debated Robert Hayne of South Carolina in 1830; Hayne defended states’ rights and nullification
Won _Dartmouth College v. Woodward_ (1819): “It is, sir, as I have said, a small college. And yet there are those who love it!”
As secretary of state, signed an 1842 treaty with Lord Ashburton settling the Maine–New Brunswick border
Secretary of state under William Henry Harrison and John Tyler (1841–1843) and again under Millard Fillmore (1850–1852)
Defends farmer Jabez Stone against the devil, Mr. Scratch, in a short story by Stephen Vincent Benét
Helped Henry Clay found the Whig Party to oppose Andrew Jackson
The only cabinet member who stayed when John Tyler’s cabinet resigned over his bank vetoes in 1841
John Greenleaf Whittier attacked him in the poem “Ichabod” (1850) after the Seventh of March speech
Argued and won _McCulloch v. Maryland_ (1819) for the national bank and _Gibbons v. Ogden_ (1824) for Gibbons
Gave the speeches at the Bunker Hill Monument’s cornerstone laying (1825) and its dedication (1843)
Ran as one of several Whig presidential candidates in 1836 but carried only Massachusetts
Praised in John F. Kennedy’s _Profiles in Courage_; a 1957 Senate committee named him one of the five greatest senators
The debate with Hayne began over Samuel Foot’s resolution on western land sales; Vice President Calhoun presided
As a New Hampshire Federalist congressman, opposed the War of 1812 and a plan to draft soldiers (1814)
Born in Salisbury, New Hampshire (1782); graduated from Dartmouth College (1801)
Died at his farm in Marshfield, Massachusetts, in 1852, a few months after Henry Clay
His 1842 treaty ended the dispute behind the bloodless “Aroostook War” and set up joint patrols against the slave trade
George P. A. Healy’s huge painting of his reply to Hayne hangs in Boston’s Faneuil Hall
His statue represents New Hampshire in the National Statuary Hall collection

trap.title: Daniel, not Noah
trap.body: Two famous Websters lived at the same time. Noah Webster wrote the first great American dictionary (1828) and the “Blue-Backed Speller,” while Daniel Webster was the Massachusetts senator and orator, so naming the wrong one loses the tossup. Some questions also want something named for him instead of the man himself: the Webster–Hayne debate, the Webster–Ashburton Treaty, or Stephen Vincent Benét’s story “The Devil and Daniel Webster.”
trap.fix: Dictionaries and spelling books mean Noah; speeches, the Senate, and Supreme Court cases mean Daniel. If you know it is a Webster, say the full name, “Daniel Webster.” Listen for “this debate,” “this treaty,” or “this story” before you buzz with the person.
trap.line: Real answer line: Daniel Webster (do not accept “Noah Webster”)

topics.name: Davy Crockett
topics.kicker: Tennessee frontiersman and congressman · Died defending the Alamo
topics.briefing: Davy Crockett was a real Tennessee frontiersman who became a legend while he was still alive. After scouting in the Creek War and serving three terms in Congress, where he broke with President Andrew Jackson by voting against the Indian Removal Act, he lost his seat, went to Texas, and died at the Alamo in 1836. A 1950s Disney TV show called him the “King of the Wild Frontier” and set off a craze for coonskin caps.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: James Kirke Paulding’s play _The Lion of the West_ starred Colonel Nimrod Wildfire, a loud, boastful backwoodsman whom audiences took to be a portrait of this congressman. The play helped make this man a national celebrity in the early 1830s.
tossups.r: A Disney show later called him the “King of the Wild Frontier.” For 10 points, name this Tennessee frontiersman who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: This man lost his 1835 reelection race to Adam Huntsman, a lawyer with a wooden leg who supported President Andrew Jackson. Four years earlier, he had also lost his seat after breaking with Jackson.
tossups.r: After his 1835 defeat, he left for Texas. For 10 points, name this congressman who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: In the Tennessee legislature and in Congress, this man fought for poor squatters in the western part of his state, hoping to let them buy the land they farmed cheaply. He first won a seat in the state legislature in 1821.
tossups.r: He later died at the Alamo. For 10 points, name this frontiersman nicknamed the “King of the Wild Frontier.”

tossups.p: In 1834, Whig politicians sponsored this man’s speaking tour of Northern cities such as Philadelphia, New York, and Boston, hoping to use his fame against President Andrew Jackson. That same year, he published an autobiography.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Tennessee congressman and frontiersman who died at the Alamo in 1836.

tossups.p: Breaking with President Andrew Jackson, this Tennessee congressman voted against the Indian Removal Act in 1830. Years earlier, he had served as a scout under Jackson’s command in the Creek War.
tossups.r: A 1950s Disney show later made him a hero to a new generation. For 10 points, name this frontiersman who died defending the Alamo.

tossups.p: This hunter claimed in his autobiography to have killed more than a hundred bears in less than a year. He represented western Tennessee in Congress for three terms, though not all in a row.
tossups.r: A popular song says he “kilt him a b’ar when he was only three.” For 10 points, name this frontiersman who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: This man’s 1834 autobiography, written while he served in Congress, includes his motto, “Be always sure you’re right, then go ahead.” The book tells of his childhood, his hunting trips, and his service in the Creek War.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Tennessee frontiersman who died at the Alamo in 1836.

tossups.p: Tall tales in almanacs bearing this man’s name claimed he could grin a raccoon out of a tree and once came home with a piece of sunrise in his pocket. Those almanacs kept appearing for about twenty years after his death.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this real frontiersman from Tennessee who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: In a 1950s Disney TV series, Fess Parker played this man and Buddy Ebsen played his friend George Russel. Disney later edited the show’s first three episodes into a 1955 movie.
tossups.r: The show set off a craze for coonskin caps. For 10 points, name this “King of the Wild Frontier,” who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: John Wayne directed and starred as this man in a 1960 film shot on a replica set near Brackettville, Texas, and Billy Bob Thornton played him in a 2004 film about the same battle.
tossups.r: He reached that battle’s fort in February 1836. For 10 points, name this frontiersman who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: This man was born in 1786 near the Nolichucky [“nah-lih-CHUH-kee”] River, in what is now Greene County in the eastern part of his state. He later moved west, and voters there sent him to the state legislature and then to Congress.
tossups.r: He was later called the “King of the Wild Frontier.” For 10 points, name this Tennessee congressman who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: A national forest in East Texas is named for this man, as are counties in both Texas and Tennessee. He had moved to Texas after his political career in Tennessee ended.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this frontiersman who died defending the Alamo against Antonio López de Santa Anna’s Mexican army.

tossups.p: In a January 1836 letter to his family, this man called Texas “the garden spot of the world.” That same month, he signed an oath of loyalty to the provisional government of Texas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this frontiersman, known as the “King of the Wild Frontier,” who died weeks later at the Alamo.

tossups.p: An account attributed to the Mexican officer José Enrique de la Peña [“deh lah PEN-yah”] claims that this man was captured alive at the end of a battle and then executed on Santa Anna’s orders. Historians still argue over how he died.
tossups.r: After leaving Congress, he went to Texas. For 10 points, name this frontiersman who died at the Alamo.

tossups.p: Bill Hayes’s recording of a song about this man reached number one on the pop charts in 1955, and Fess Parker, who played him on television, also recorded it. The song was written for a Disney TV show, and several other singers recorded it too.
tossups.r: That song begins “Born on a mountain top in Tennessee.” For 10 points, name this frontiersman who died at the Alamo.

trap.title: Crockett, Boone, or Bowie?
trap.body: Fess Parker played both Davy Crockett and Daniel Boone on TV in a coonskin cap, so the two frontiersmen get mixed up. Boone explored Kentucky through the Cumberland Gap and founded Boonesborough; Crockett was a Tennessee congressman who died at the Alamo. At the Alamo itself, Crockett died alongside Jim Bowie, of the Bowie knife, and William Travis, who commanded the Texan defenders, and some tossups ask for the battle instead of the man.
trap.fix: Tennessee, Congress, the vote against the Indian Removal Act, and “King of the Wild Frontier” mean Crockett. Kentucky and the Wilderness Road mean Boone. The famous knife means Bowie, and the “Victory or Death” letter means Travis. If the question says “this battle,” answer the Alamo.

topics.name: Donner Party
topics.kicker: Pioneers trapped in the Sierra Nevada snow · The winter of 1846–47
topics.briefing: In 1846, the families of George and Jacob Donner and James Reed left Springfield, Illinois, for California, and others joined them along the way. They gambled on a “shortcut” that cost them weeks, and early blizzards trapped them in the Sierra Nevada beside a lake now called Donner Lake. Rescue parties struggled through deep snow all winter, but nearly half of the group died before the last survivor was brought out in April 1847.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1847, Mormon pioneers led by Brigham Young followed a rough wagon road that this group had spent weeks cutting through the Wasatch [“WAH-satch”] Mountains the year before. Delays like that one left this group far behind schedule.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers who were trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in the winter of 1846 to 1847.

tossups.p: When this group reached Fort Bridger in 1846, they learned that the guide they had counted on had already gone ahead with another wagon train. They decided to follow his route anyway, south of the Great Salt Lake.
tossups.r: That guide was Lansford Hastings. For 10 points, name this group that took the Hastings Cutoff and became trapped in the Sierra Nevada.

tossups.p: At Fort Laramie, the mountain man James Clyman warned one of this group’s leaders, an old friend, not to take a shortcut that had never been tried with wagons. That leader, James Reed, ignored the advice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of California-bound emigrants who took the Hastings Cutoff and were trapped by snow in 1846.

tossups.p: This group was formed in July 1846 at the Little Sandy River, in what is now Wyoming, when the families who planned to take a new shortcut chose their own captain. Its leading families had started out from Springfield, Illinois, that April.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this wagon train, named for its captain, that was trapped in the Sierra Nevada.

tossups.p: James Reed’s family had to abandon their two-level wagon, later nicknamed the “Pioneer Palace Car,” after most of their oxen were lost crossing a salt desert that proved about twice as wide as promised.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers whose survivors reached California in 1847 after a winter trapped in the Sierra Nevada.

tossups.p: Eight-year-old Patty Reed hid a tiny wooden doll in her clothes throughout this group’s ordeal, and it is displayed at Sutter’s Fort in Sacramento. Her father led the second relief party to reach this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers trapped near a lake in the Sierra Nevada in 1846 and 1847.

tossups.p: Tamsen, the wife of this group’s elected captain, refused to leave her dying husband at their camp on Alder Creek, and she sent her young daughters out with rescuers instead. Neither she nor her husband survived.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada on the way to California.

tossups.p: Patrick Breen kept a diary through the winter that this group spent in crude cabins beside Truckee Lake. His entries record snowstorms, hunger, and prayers for rescue, and his whole family survived.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers whose winter camp was beside a lake later renamed for them.

tossups.p: Charles Stanton rode ahead to Sutter’s Fort and returned to this group with mules carrying food in October 1846. Two months later, he died in the mountains while trying to lead a party out on snowshoes.
tossups.r: That party was the Forlorn Hope. For 10 points, name this group of pioneers trapped in the Sierra Nevada.

tossups.p: In April 1847, the fourth and last relief party found Lewis Keseberg alone at this group’s lake camp, the final survivor to be rescued. Months earlier, the Mexican-American War had pulled many men away from California’s settlements, slowing rescue efforts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of emigrants trapped in the Sierra Nevada in the winter of 1846 to 1847.

tossups.p: In January 1847, William Eddy staggered into Johnson’s Ranch to call for help, the first to arrive of the only seven snowshoers who survived the trek out of the mountains. His group had left the lake camp a month earlier.
tossups.r: That group was called the Forlorn Hope. For 10 points, name this group of pioneers trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada.

tossups.p: In a May 1847 letter to her cousin, 13-year-old Virginia Reed wrote that she had not told half of their troubles, and she gave this advice: “Never take no cutoffs and hurry along as fast as you can.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers whose disastrous shortcut left them trapped in the Sierra Nevada.

tossups.p: Along the Humboldt River, James Reed killed the teamster John Snyder in a fight, and the rest of this group banished Reed. He rode ahead to California, where he later organized a relief party to rescue his family.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in 1846.

tossups.p: A statue of a pioneer family at a California state park stands on a base 22 feet tall, said to match the depth of the snow that buried this group’s camp. That park sits beside a lake once called Truckee Lake.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers trapped in the Sierra Nevada in 1846 and 1847.

tossups.p: The Central Pacific Railroad and, later, Interstate 80 crossed the Sierra Nevada near a pass named for this group. In 1844, the Stephens–Townsend–Murphy Party had become the first to bring wagons over that pass.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of pioneers who failed to cross the Sierra Nevada before winter snows trapped them in 1846.

trap.title: Party, pass, or trail?
trap.body: Several places are named for this group, including Donner Lake, Donner Pass, and Donner Memorial State Park, so make sure the question wants the people. Other questions about westward travel want the Oregon Trail or the California Trail, which the Donner Party was following before it took the Hastings Cutoff, and some ask for that “shortcut” itself or for the snowshoe group called the Forlorn Hope.
trap.fix: “This group,” “this party,” or “these emigrants” means the Donner Party. “This pass” means Donner Pass, and “this route” or “this shortcut” may mean the Hastings Cutoff. Clues about Oregon’s Willamette Valley or the Whitman Mission point to the Oregon Trail.
trap.line: Real answer line: Donner Party (accept Donner–Reed Party; prompt on Donner)

topics.name: Dred Scott v. Sandford
topics.kicker: 1857 Supreme Court slavery case · Struck down the Missouri Compromise
topics.briefing: Dred Scott was an enslaved man whose owner had taken him to live in places where slavery was banned, so he and his wife, Harriet, sued for their freedom. In 1857, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 against him: Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote that Black Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, so the Missouri Compromise was unconstitutional. The ruling deepened the split between North and South.
topics.answerHtml: Dred Scott v. Sandford (accept Scott v. Sandford or the spelling “Sanford”; prompt on Scott)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Less than three months after this case was decided, Taylor Blow, the son of the plaintiff’s first owner, freed the plaintiff and his family. The plaintiff died of tuberculosis in St. Louis the following year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 Supreme Court case in which Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens.

tossups.p: Newspapers embarrassed Calvin Chaffee, an antislavery congressman from Massachusetts, by pointing out that his wife was the widow of John Emerson, who had owned the plaintiff in this case. Emerson, an army surgeon, had taken the plaintiff to Illinois and to Fort Snelling.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 case that ruled Congress could not ban slavery in the territories.

tossups.p: Shortly before this case was decided, President-elect James Buchanan privately urged Justice Robert Grier, a fellow Pennsylvanian, to join the majority. In his inaugural address two days before the ruling, Buchanan said that the Supreme Court would soon settle the question of slavery in the territories.
tossups.r: It ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens. For 10 points, name this case decided by Roger Taney’s [“TAW-neez”] court in March 1857.

tossups.p: In a dissent, Justice Benjamin Curtis pointed out that free Black men could vote in five of the original states when the nation was founded. John McLean also dissented, and Curtis resigned from the Court later that year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 7–2 decision by Chief Justice Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] that struck down the Missouri Compromise.

tossups.p: Montgomery Blair, who later served as Abraham Lincoln’s postmaster general, argued the plaintiff’s side when this case reached the Supreme Court. The justices heard arguments twice, in February and December 1856.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 case in which the Court ruled against an enslaved man who sued for his freedom.

tossups.p: The official name of this case misspells the name of its defendant, John Sanford, the brother of army surgeon John Emerson’s widow. The plaintiff sued Sanford in federal court because Sanford lived in another state, New York.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 case in which Chief Justice Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] ruled against the enslaved plaintiff.

tossups.p: The plaintiff in this case married Harriet Robinson at Fort Snelling, in what is now Minnesota, where the Missouri Compromise had banned slavery. His owner, army surgeon John Emerson, had also taken him to live in the free state of Illinois.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 Supreme Court case in which the plaintiff lost his bid for freedom.

tossups.p: In 1850, a jury in St. Louis decided that the plaintiff in this case and his wife were free, but the Missouri Supreme Court reversed that ruling two years later. The couple had first sued for their freedom in 1846 at St. Louis’s Old Courthouse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this case that the U.S. Supreme Court decided against the plaintiff in 1857.

tossups.p: In his “House Divided” speech, Abraham Lincoln suggested that four men he called “Stephen, Franklin, Roger, and James” had worked together to spread slavery, pointing to this case as evidence. “Roger” was the Chief Justice who wrote this case’s majority opinion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 decision that Lincoln and Stephen Douglas argued over during their 1858 debates.

tossups.p: At Freeport, Illinois, Stephen Douglas argued that settlers could still keep slavery out of a territory by refusing to pass laws protecting it, despite this ruling. That answer to Abraham Lincoln’s question cost Douglas support among Southern Democrats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 Supreme Court case that declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.

tossups.p: In 2012, a bronze statue of the plaintiff in this case and his wife, Harriet, was unveiled outside the Old Courthouse in St. Louis, where their fight for freedom began. That courthouse is part of Gateway Arch National Park.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 case in which the Supreme Court ruled that Black Americans could not be citizens.

tossups.p: This ruling was only the second time the Supreme Court had struck down a federal law, more than fifty years after _Marbury v. Madison_. The law it struck down had already been repealed by the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854.
tossups.r: That law was the Missouri Compromise. For 10 points, name this 1857 case decided by Roger Taney’s [“TAW-neez”] court.

tossups.p: This ruling’s majority opinion argued that enslaved people were property protected by the Fifth Amendment’s due process clause, and that the plaintiff’s years on free soil had not made him free under Missouri law.
tossups.r: It also said Black Americans could not be citizens. For 10 points, name this 1857 Supreme Court case.

tossups.p: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, overturned part of this ruling by declaring that all persons born or naturalized in the United States are citizens. The Thirteenth Amendment had already ended slavery three years earlier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1857 case in which Chief Justice Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”] said Black Americans could not be citizens.

tossups.p: The author of this ruling’s majority opinion had been named Chief Justice by Andrew Jackson after John Marshall died. That justice was also the brother-in-law of Francis Scott Key, who wrote the words of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”
tossups.r: That justice was Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”]. For 10 points, name this 1857 case that declared the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional.

Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote the majority opinion

The lawsuit began in 1846 at St. Louis’s Old Courthouse; a jury freed the couple in 1850, but the Missouri Supreme Court reversed it in 1852
Taylor Blow, son of the plaintiff’s first owner, freed the family in May 1857; the plaintiff died of tuberculosis in 1858

trap.title: Not Plessy, not Taney
trap.body: Several famous Supreme Court cases about race get mixed up. _Dred Scott v. Sandford_ (1857) said Black Americans could not be citizens and struck down the Missouri Compromise; _Plessy v. Ferguson_ (1896) allowed “separate but equal” segregation; and _Brown v. Board of Education_ (1954) overturned Plessy for public schools. Some tossups instead ask for the man who wrote the opinion, Roger Taney, or for the law the case struck down, the Missouri Compromise.
trap.fix: Listen for the date and the noun: 1857 and “this case” or “this decision” mean Dred Scott, while “this Chief Justice” means Taney and “this law” or “this agreement” means the Missouri Compromise. The defendant’s name is often spelled “Sanford,” and both spellings are accepted.
trap.line: Real answer line: Dred Scott v. Sandford (accept Scott v. Sandford or the spelling “Sanford”; prompt on Scott)

topics.name: Emancipation Proclamation
topics.kicker: Lincoln’s order freeing enslaved people · Took effect January 1, 1863
topics.briefing: On New Year’s Day 1863, Abraham Lincoln signed an order declaring that enslaved people in the states rebelling against the Union “are, and henceforward shall be free.” Because it applied only to areas the Confederacy controlled, freedom often arrived only when Union soldiers did. The order also let Black men join the Union Army and Navy, and nearly 200,000 served before the war ended.
topics.answerHtml: Emancipation Proclamation (prompt on emancipation or proclamation; do not accept “Thirteenth Amendment”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On July 22, 1862, the President read a draft of this document to his cabinet, and Secretary of State William Seward advised waiting to issue it until the Union won a major victory. That victory came two months later in Maryland.
tossups.r: Five days after the Battle of Antietam, Abraham Lincoln announced this order. For 10 points, name this document that took effect on January 1, 1863.

tossups.p: A month before announcing this order, its author replied to Horace Greeley’s editorial “The Prayer of Twenty Millions” by writing, “If I could save the Union without freeing any slave I would do it.” He had already drafted this order by then.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this order by Abraham Lincoln that declared enslaved people in the rebelling states to be free.

tossups.p: Francis Bicknell Carpenter spent six months at the White House painting the President and his cabinet at the first reading of this document. That 1864 painting hangs in the U.S. Capitol, and Carpenter later wrote a book about his stay.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this order, issued by Abraham Lincoln, that took effect on January 1, 1863.

tossups.p: On December 31, 1862, many Black churches held “Watch Night” services, staying up past midnight in prayer and celebration. The next day, Frederick Douglass waited with a crowd at Boston’s Tremont Temple for word from Washington.
tossups.r: They were waiting for this order to take effect. For 10 points, name this order by Abraham Lincoln that freed enslaved people in the rebelling states.

tossups.p: In 1861 and 1862, the President overruled generals John C. Frémont [“FREE-mont”] and David Hunter, who had each declared enslaved people free in areas under their command. He later issued his own order as a war measure, using his powers as commander in chief.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this order that Abraham Lincoln issued after the Battle of Antietam.

tossups.p: In April 1862, Congress freed enslaved people in Washington, D.C., and paid their owners, months before the President issued this broader order. That summer, the Second Confiscation Act declared free any enslaved people of rebel owners who escaped to Union lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this order, announced in September 1862, that took effect on January 1, 1863.

tossups.p: After shaking hands for hours at a White House reception, the President worried that his tired hand would make his signature on this document look shaky. As he signed, he reportedly said, “If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act.”
tossups.r: It applied only to areas in rebellion. For 10 points, name this order that Abraham Lincoln signed on January 1, 1863.

tossups.p: The original of this document, five pages long, is kept at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. Because light can damage it, it is shown to the public for only a few days each year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 order by Abraham Lincoln that freed enslaved people in Confederate-held areas.

tossups.p: This order exempted Tennessee, the 48 counties that became West Virginia, and Union-held parts of Louisiana and Virginia, including New Orleans and Norfolk. Its preliminary version had given the rebelling states about 100 days to rejoin the Union.
tossups.r: It also did not apply in the border states. For 10 points, name this 1863 order by Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: This order ends by calling itself “an act of justice, warranted by the Constitution, upon military necessity,” and asks for “the considerate judgment of mankind, and the gracious favor of Almighty God.”
tossups.r: Abraham Lincoln issued it as a war measure. For 10 points, name this order that took effect on January 1, 1863.

tossups.p: After this order took effect, Frederick Douglass published the call “Men of Color, To Arms!” and helped recruit soldiers for the 54th Massachusetts, in which two of his sons enlisted.
tossups.r: This order let Black men join the Union Army and Navy. For 10 points, name this order issued by Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: On June 19, 1865, in Galveston, Texas, Union general Gordon Granger issued General Order No. 3, announcing that all enslaved people in Texas were free under this earlier order. That day is remembered as Juneteenth.
tossups.r: Juneteenth became a federal holiday in 2021. For 10 points, name this order by Abraham Lincoln that took effect on January 1, 1863.

tossups.p: Cotton workers in Manchester, England, sent the President a letter praising this order even though a cotton shortage caused by the war had left many of them out of work. He wrote back to thank them.
tossups.r: This order made Britain and France less likely to back the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this order announced after the Battle of Antietam.

tossups.p: The preliminary version of this order warned that enslaved people in any state still rebelling on a set date “shall be then, thenceforward, and forever free.” It also repeated the President’s offer of money to loyal states that chose to end slavery themselves.
tossups.r: That version came five days after the Battle of Antietam. For 10 points, name this order by Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: The final version of this order declared that enslaved people in the listed areas “are, and henceforward shall be free,” and that freed men would be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts and to man ships.
tossups.r: Nearly 200,000 Black men served in the Union Army and Navy by the war’s end. For 10 points, name this order signed by Abraham Lincoln on January 1, 1863.

trap.title: Proclamation or amendment?
trap.body: The Emancipation Proclamation (1863) was a wartime order by Lincoln that freed enslaved people only in areas still in rebellion. The Thirteenth Amendment (ratified 1865) abolished slavery everywhere in the United States, so naming one for the other loses the tossup. Juneteenth, the Gettysburg Address, and the Confiscation Acts share clues with it too, and Russia’s 1861 Emancipation Manifesto freed serfs, not enslaved Americans.
trap.fix: Listen for the type of thing: “this order,” “this proclamation,” or “this document” issued by Lincoln in 1862 or 1863 means the Emancipation Proclamation; “this amendment” ratified in 1865 means the Thirteenth Amendment. A date of June 19, 1865, means Juneteenth.
trap.line: Real answer line: Emancipation Proclamation (prompt on emancipation or proclamation; do not accept “Thirteenth Amendment”)

topics.name: Fort Sumter
topics.kicker: Charleston Harbor fort · Where the Civil War began in April 1861
topics.briefing: After South Carolina left the Union, Major Robert Anderson and fewer than a hundred U.S. soldiers held Fort Sumter, an unfinished fort on a man-made island guarding the harbor of Charleston, South Carolina. At 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, Confederate cannons opened fire, and after 34 hours Anderson surrendered. Nobody was killed by the bombardment itself, but it started the Civil War.
topics.answerHtml: Fort Sumter (accept Battle of Fort Sumter; prompt on Charleston Harbor)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Construction of this fort began in 1829 on a man-made island built from tons of granite and other rock, and it was still unfinished more than thirty years later. Its walls were designed to hold more than a hundred cannons.
tossups.r: Robert Anderson commanded this fort in 1861. For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor where the Civil War began.

tossups.p: This fort was named for a South Carolina general of the Revolutionary War nicknamed “the Carolina Gamecock.” It was built after the War of 1812 to guard the entrance to an important Southern harbor.
tossups.r: Confederate guns attacked it on April 12, 1861. For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor.

tossups.p: Six days after South Carolina seceded, the commander of the U.S. Army post there secretly moved his men to this fort from Fort Moultrie [“MOOL-tree”], which could easily be attacked from land. He moved them at night, on December 26, 1860.
tossups.r: That commander was Major Robert Anderson. For 10 points, name this fort where the Civil War began.

tossups.p: In January 1861, cadets from The Citadel fired on the _Star of the West_, an unarmed merchant ship carrying soldiers and supplies to this fort, and the ship turned back. President James Buchanan had sent that ship.
tossups.r: Three months later, Confederate cannons fired on this fort. For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor.

tossups.p: In April 1861, President Lincoln informed South Carolina governor Francis Pickens that he would send only food, not soldiers or weapons, to this fort’s hungry garrison. Confederate leaders decided to attack before the supplies arrived.
tossups.r: General P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”] then ordered the bombardment. For 10 points, name this fort where the Civil War began.

tossups.p: Gustavus Fox led a relief fleet that arrived outside the harbor during the attack on this fort, but it could not reach the fort in time to help. Fox later became assistant secretary of the navy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor where the Civil War began in April 1861.

tossups.p: The Confederate general who ordered the attack on this fort had once studied artillery at West Point under the Union officer defending it, and later served as his assistant there. That Union officer was a Kentucky native.
tossups.r: Those men were P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”] and Robert Anderson. For 10 points, name this fort where the Civil War began.

tossups.p: At 4:30 a.m., a signal shell fired from Fort Johnson burst over this fort, starting a bombardment. The Virginia secessionist Edmund Ruffin is often said to have fired one of the first shots that followed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort attacked on April 12, 1861, at the start of the Civil War.

tossups.p: Mary Chesnut wrote in her diary that she knelt and prayed when the guns began firing at this fort, then watched from a rooftop in the nearby city. Her husband, James, was one of the aides who carried the demand that the fort surrender.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor whose bombardment began the Civil War.

tossups.p: Captain Abner Doubleday, who was later wrongly credited with inventing baseball, aimed the first shot fired back by the defenders of this fort. The garrison was running out of food and could use only some of its cannons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort that surrendered after a 34-hour bombardment in April 1861.

tossups.p: During a salute to the U.S. flag after this fort surrendered, a pile of cartridges blew up by accident, killing Private Daniel Hough. Not one person had died during the 34-hour bombardment before the surrender.
tossups.r: Hough is often called the first soldier to die in the Civil War. For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor.

tossups.p: Three days after the attack on this fort began, Abraham Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers to put down the rebellion. That call led Virginia, Arkansas, North Carolina, and Tennessee to leave the Union.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor that Confederates captured at the start of the Civil War.

tossups.p: In April 1863, Union ironclads under Samuel Du Pont failed to capture this fort, and later Union guns pounded it into rubble. Confederates held it until February 1865, when they abandoned the nearby city as William Tecumseh Sherman’s army marched through South Carolina.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort where the Civil War had begun almost four years earlier.

tossups.p: On April 14, 1865, Henry Ward Beecher gave a speech as this fort’s former commander raised over it the same flag he had lowered exactly four years earlier. That night, Abraham Lincoln was shot at Ford’s Theatre.
tossups.r: That commander was Robert Anderson. For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor.

tossups.p: The day after U.S. troops secretly moved into this fort, South Carolina militia seized Castle Pinckney and the abandoned Fort Moultrie [“MOOL-tree”] nearby. Over the next months, Southern troops built gun batteries around the harbor aimed at this fort.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this fort in Charleston Harbor where the first shots of the Civil War were fired.
