trap.title: Sumter, not Moultrie or McHenry
trap.body: Charleston Harbor had several forts. Robert Anderson’s men started out at Fort Moultrie and moved to Fort Sumter in December 1860, and Confederate guns at Moultrie and Fort Johnson later fired on Sumter. Players also mix up Fort Sumter (1861, the Civil War) with Fort McHenry (1814, the War of 1812 and “The Star-Spangled Banner”) and with Fort Sumner in New Mexico, where Navajo people were held after the Long Walk.
trap.fix: The Civil War, April 1861, Anderson, and Beauregard mean Sumter. The War of 1812 and the national anthem mean McHenry. If a clue says troops moved out of a fort in December 1860, that fort was Moultrie; the fort they moved into is Sumter.
trap.line: Real answer line: Fort Sumter (accept Battle of Fort Sumter; prompt on Charleston Harbor)

topics.name: Francis Scott Key
topics.kicker: Lawyer and poet · Wrote the words of “The Star-Spangled Banner”
topics.briefing: In September 1814, a Maryland lawyer named Francis Scott Key was stuck on a boat behind a British fleet as it bombarded Fort McHenry in Baltimore through a rainy night. In the morning he saw a huge American flag still flying over the fort and wrote a poem about it. Set to a popular British tune, the poem became “The Star-Spangled Banner,” which Congress made the national anthem in 1931.
topics.answerHtml: Francis Scott Key (do not accept “The Star-Spangled Banner”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1805, this man wrote a song honoring the naval hero Stephen Decatur, set to the same British tune he later used for his most famous poem. That tune, “To Anacreon [“uh-NAK-ree-un”] in Heaven,” was written for a London gentlemen’s club.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who wrote the words to “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: With the prisoner-exchange agent John Stuart Skinner, this lawyer boarded a British warship to win the release of Dr. William Beanes, an elderly doctor from Maryland. The British let Beanes go but held all three men until they had finished a planned attack.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man who watched the bombardment of Fort McHenry and wrote “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: As U.S. attorney for Washington, D.C., this man prosecuted Richard Lawrence, who had tried to shoot President Andrew Jackson in 1835. Lawrence was found not guilty by reason of insanity.
tossups.r: Two decades earlier, this lawyer wrote a poem during the War of 1812. For 10 points, name this author of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: This man helped found the American Colonization Society in 1816, a group that urged free Black Americans to move to Africa and later founded Liberia. He enslaved people himself, though as a lawyer he also represented some enslaved people suing for their freedom.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Maryland lawyer who wrote “Defence of Fort M’Henry,” the poem that became the national anthem.

tossups.p: This man’s sister Anne married Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”], making this man the brother-in-law of the Chief Justice who later wrote the _Dred Scott_ decision. Taney later wrote an account of how this man came to write his most famous poem.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who watched the British attack Fort McHenry in 1814 and wrote a poem about it.

tossups.p: This man was born in 1779 at Terra Rubra, his family’s estate in Maryland, and he is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Frederick, where a U.S. flag flies over his grave day and night.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who wrote the words to the U.S. national anthem.

tossups.p: The Baltimore music seller Thomas Carr published this man’s best-known poem as sheet music in 1814, giving it a new title. The poem had first been printed on handbills under the title “Defence of Fort M’Henry.”
tossups.r: Carr’s title was “The Star-Spangled Banner.” For 10 points, name this lawyer who wrote it.

tossups.p: The U.S. Navy adopted this man’s best-known work for official use in 1889, and in 1916 Woodrow Wilson ordered it played at military and other official events. Its words come from this man’s four-stanza poem, though usually only the first stanza is sung.
tossups.r: Congress made it the national anthem in 1931. For 10 points, name this lawyer who wrote “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: Major George Armistead [“AR-mih-sted”] asked for a flag so large that the British would have no trouble seeing it from a distance, and Mary Pickersgill and her helpers sewed one with fifteen stars and fifteen stripes. That flag is displayed at the Smithsonian.
tossups.r: Seeing it still flying over Fort McHenry inspired this man’s famous poem. For 10 points, name this author of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: The novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald, author of _The Great Gatsby_, was named after this distant relative. A bridge across the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., also honors this man, who once lived in nearby Georgetown.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Maryland lawyer who wrote the words of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: In March 2024, a cargo ship lost power and struck a support of a Baltimore bridge named for this man, and the bridge collapsed into the Patapsco [“puh-TAP-skoh”] River. Six road workers on the bridge died.
tossups.r: That bridge crossed the river near where this man watched a British attack in 1814. For 10 points, name this author of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: During the attack this man witnessed, British ships, including the rocket ship HMS _Erebus_, fired Congreve rockets and huge bombs at a fort for about twenty-five hours. _Erebus_ was later lost on John Franklin’s expedition to the Arctic.
tossups.r: This man later described “the rockets’ red glare” in a poem. For 10 points, name this author of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: Six days after the battle that inspired it, this man’s best-known poem was printed in a Baltimore newspaper, and within weeks many other newspapers had reprinted it. He is said to have begun the poem on the back of a letter he was carrying.
tossups.r: He had watched the British bombard Fort McHenry from a boat during a rainy night. For 10 points, name this man who wrote the words of “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: A day before the bombardment this man watched, British general Robert Ross was killed at the Battle of North Point as his army marched toward a major port. Weeks earlier, Ross’s troops had burned Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who wrote “Defence of Fort M’Henry,” better known as “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

tossups.p: The fourth stanza of this man’s most famous poem includes the line “And this be our motto: ‘In God is our trust.’” Most people know only the first of the poem’s four stanzas.
tossups.r: That first stanza begins “O say can you see.” For 10 points, name this lawyer whose poem became “The Star-Spangled Banner.”

clues.t: Wrote the poem that became “The Star-Spangled Banner,” the U.S. national anthem
Watched the British bombard Fort McHenry in Baltimore in September 1814, during the War of 1812
Was inspired by seeing the huge American flag still flying over the fort the next morning
A Maryland lawyer and amateur poet
The poem was first printed on handbills as “Defence of Fort M’Henry”
Set to the tune of “To Anacreon in Heaven,” by British composer John Stafford Smith
Congress made the song the national anthem in 1931; President Herbert Hoover signed the law
Went to the British fleet to win the release of Dr. William Beanes, an elderly Maryland doctor
The fort’s giant flag, with 15 stars and 15 stripes, was sewn by Mary Pickersgill and is displayed at the Smithsonian
Was held on a small American boat behind the British fleet during the rainy, all-night attack
The poem has four stanzas; usually only the first, beginning “O say can you see,” is sung
A Baltimore bridge named for him collapsed in March 2024 after a cargo ship struck it; six workers died
Went to the British with prisoner-exchange agent John Stuart Skinner
Major George Armistead, the fort’s commander, wanted a flag big enough for the British to see from a distance
Brother-in-law of Chief Justice Roger Taney, who later wrote the _Dred Scott_ decision
As U.S. attorney for Washington, D.C., prosecuted Richard Lawrence, who tried to shoot Andrew Jackson (1835)
Helped found the American Colonization Society (1816); he enslaved people but also argued some freedom suits
In 1805 he wrote a song for naval hero Stephen Decatur, set to the same tune
The Navy adopted the song in 1889; Woodrow Wilson ordered it played at official events in 1916
Born in 1779 at Terra Rubra, Maryland; buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Frederick, where a flag flies day and night
Baltimore music seller Thomas Carr first published it as sheet music under the title “The Star-Spangled Banner”
Novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald was named after him, a distant relative
Lived in Georgetown; a bridge across the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., is also named for him
British ships, including the rocket ship HMS _Erebus_, fired Congreve rockets during the attack (“the rockets’ red glare”)
General Robert Ross, who had burned Washington, was killed at North Point the day before the bombardment
The fourth stanza says, “And this be our motto: ‘In God is our trust’”

trap.title: Poet, poem, or fort?
trap.body: Francis Scott Key wrote the words, but many tossups ask for the song itself, “The Star-Spangled Banner” (first printed as “Defence of Fort M’Henry”), or for the fort, Fort McHenry, or the war, the War of 1812. On this answer line, naming the song is wrong, the same way naming the fort or the war would be. Don’t confuse him with F. Scott Fitzgerald, the novelist who was named after him, or with Mary Pickersgill, who sewed the flag.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this man,” “this lawyer,” or “this poet” wants Key; “this song” or “this poem” wants “The Star-Spangled Banner”; “this fort” wants Fort McHenry. The tune was composed by John Stafford Smith, not Key.
trap.line: Real answer line: Francis Scott Key (do not accept “The Star-Spangled Banner”)

topics.name: George W. Bush
topics.kicker: 43rd U.S. President · Led the nation after the September 11 attacks
topics.briefing: In 2000, the whole presidential election came down to Florida, where George W. Bush finished just 537 votes ahead of Al Gore after weeks of recounts that the Supreme Court halted in _Bush v. Gore_. Bush and his father, George H. W. Bush, became the second father and son to both serve as president, after John and John Quincy Adams. Less than eight months into his first term, the September 11 attacks reshaped his presidency.
topics.answerHtml: George Walker Bush (or George W. Bush; accept Bush 43 or Dubya; prompt on Bush or George Bush; do not accept “George H. W. Bush” or “Jeb Bush”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man lost a 1978 race for Congress in West Texas and spent years in the oil business in Midland. In 1989, he joined a group of investors that bought baseball’s Texas Rangers, and he served as the team’s managing general partner.
tossups.r: He later defeated Ann Richards to become governor of Texas. For 10 points, name this man who became the 43rd president.

tossups.p: This man flew F-102 fighter jets in the Texas Air National Guard after graduating from Yale, and he later became the first U.S. president with a Master of Business Administration degree, which he earned at Harvard in 1975.
tossups.r: His father was the 41st president. For 10 points, name this Republican who served as the 43rd president.

tossups.p: Arguments over Palm Beach County’s “butterfly ballot” and over “hanging chads” on punch-card ballots marked the disputed vote count in Florida, where this candidate was certified the winner by 537 votes. A Supreme Court case named for this man and his opponent ended the recounts in December 2000.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican who defeated Al Gore in the 2000 presidential election.

tossups.p: This president was listening to second graders read at an elementary school in Sarasota, Florida, when his chief of staff, Andrew Card, whispered to him that “America is under attack.” Three days later, he spoke to rescue workers at Ground Zero through a bullhorn.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who led the country after the September 11 attacks.

tossups.p: Former Pennsylvania governor Tom Ridge became the first secretary of a cabinet department created under this president in 2002, which brought together 22 federal agencies, including the Coast Guard and the Secret Service.
tossups.r: That department was the Department of Homeland Security. For 10 points, name this president who also signed the USA PATRIOT Act.

tossups.p: Senator Ted Kennedy worked with this Republican president to pass an education law, signed in January 2002, that required yearly reading and math tests in grades 3 through 8. Schools that did not make “adequate yearly progress” under that law faced consequences.
tossups.r: That law was called No Child Left Behind. For 10 points, name this president, whose wife, Laura, had been a school librarian.

tossups.p: This president signed a 2003 law that added prescription drug coverage, known as Part D, to Medicare. That same year, he announced PEPFAR, an emergency plan that went on to pay for HIV treatment for millions of people, especially in Africa.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who sent U.S. troops into Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks.

tossups.p: During a financial crisis late in this president’s second term, Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson asked Congress for 700 billion dollars to shore up struggling banks. This president signed the 2008 law that created that rescue fund, the Troubled Asset Relief Program, or TARP.
tossups.r: His successor was Barack Obama. For 10 points, name this president who had defeated Al Gore in 2000.

tossups.p: In May 2003, this president landed in a Navy jet on the aircraft carrier USS _Abraham Lincoln_ and gave a speech beneath a banner reading “Mission Accomplished.” That December, American troops captured Saddam Hussein [“hoo-SAYN”] near his hometown of Tikrit [“tih-KREET”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who ordered the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

tossups.p: In his 2002 State of the Union address, this president called Iran, Iraq, and North Korea an “axis of evil.” His secretary of state, Colin Powell, later presented the case against Iraq’s weapons programs to the United Nations Security Council.
tossups.r: In 2003, this president ordered the invasion of Iraq. For 10 points, name this president, whose vice president was Dick Cheney.

tossups.p: This president nominated his White House counsel, Harriet Miers, to the Supreme Court, but she withdrew, and he chose Samuel Alito instead. Earlier that year, he had named John Roberts to succeed William Rehnquist [“REN-kwist”] as Chief Justice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who won reelection over John Kerry in 2004.

tossups.p: FEMA director Michael Brown resigned after this president’s administration was widely criticized for its response to a 2005 disaster. In that disaster, levee failures flooded about 80 percent of New Orleans.
tossups.r: That disaster was Hurricane Katrina. For 10 points, name this president, who had been governor of Texas before taking office in 2001.

tossups.p: This president won reelection in 2004 by carrying Ohio, defeating a Massachusetts senator who had won a Silver Star in Vietnam. Four years earlier, he had lost the national popular vote but won the Electoral College by 271 votes to 266.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Republican who served as president from 2001 to 2009.

tossups.p: After leaving office, this man took up painting and published _Portraits of Courage_, a book of his paintings of military veterans. His presidential center opened in 2013 at Southern Methodist University in Dallas.
tossups.r: His memoir is titled _Decision Points_. For 10 points, name this former governor of Texas who became the 43rd president.

tossups.p: During his 2000 campaign, this candidate called his philosophy “compassionate conservatism.” Soon after taking office, he created a White House office to help religious and community charities compete for federal grants, the Office of Faith-Based and Community Initiatives.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 43rd president, whose brother Jeb served as governor of Florida.

clues.t: 43rd President (2001–2009), a Republican; came after Bill Clinton and before Barack Obama
Son of the 41st president; they were the second father and son presidents, after John Adams and John Quincy Adams
President during the September 11 attacks (2001)
Governor of Texas (1995–2000) before becoming president
Defeated Al Gore in the disputed election of 2000
Won Florida by 537 votes after a recount; the Supreme Court case named for him and Gore stopped the recount
Lost the national popular vote in 2000 but won the Electoral College, 271 to 266
The Department of Homeland Security was formed under him (2002); Tom Ridge was its first secretary
No Child Left Behind (signed in 2002) required yearly reading and math tests in grades 3 through 8
Sent troops into Afghanistan (2001) and ordered the invasion of Iraq (2003), which removed Saddam Hussein from power
His administration said Iraq had weapons of mass destruction; no stockpiles were found after the invasion
Hurricane Katrina (2005) flooded most of New Orleans; the federal response was widely criticized
Vice president: Dick Cheney; won reelection in 2004 over Massachusetts senator John Kerry
Signed the USA PATRIOT Act (2001), which expanded the government’s surveillance powers
Was listening to second graders read in Sarasota, Florida, when Andrew Card whispered “America is under attack”
Spoke to rescue workers at Ground Zero through a bullhorn: “I can hear you!”
Called Iran, Iraq, and North Korea an “axis of evil” in his 2002 State of the Union address
Spoke beneath a “Mission Accomplished” banner on the aircraft carrier USS _Abraham Lincoln_ (May 2003)
Signed Medicare Part D for prescription drugs (2003) and launched PEPFAR to fight HIV/AIDS abroad (2003)
Signed TARP (2008), a $700 billion fund to steady banks during a financial crisis; Henry Paulson was his Treasury Secretary
Appointed Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Samuel Alito; his nominee Harriet Miers withdrew
Managing general partner of baseball’s Texas Rangers (1989–1994); earlier worked in the oil business in Midland
First president with an MBA (Harvard, 1975); a Yale graduate who flew F-102 jets in the Texas Air National Guard
Lost a 1978 race for Congress; became governor by defeating Ann Richards in 1994
Secretaries of State Colin Powell (the first Black secretary of state) and Condoleezza Rice; Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld
Called his philosophy “compassionate conservatism”; created a White House office for faith-based charities
After office, painted veterans for _Portraits of Courage_, wrote the memoir _Decision Points_, and opened his presidential center at SMU in Dallas
Wife Laura, a former teacher and librarian, started the National Book Festival; brother Jeb was governor of Florida

trap.title: Which George Bush?
trap.body: Two presidents named George Bush appear in quiz bowl. George H. W. Bush, the father, was the 41st president (1989–1993) and led the 1991 Gulf War against Iraq; his son George W. Bush was the 43rd president (2001–2009) and ordered the invasion of Iraq in 2003. Real answer lines prompt on just “Bush” and do not accept the wrong George, so an early buzz on an Iraq clue can go wrong. A third Bush, Jeb, was governor of Florida during the 2000 recount.
trap.fix: H. W. clues: Ronald Reagan’s vice president, the CIA, “Read my lips: no new taxes,” Operation Desert Storm, and the end of the Cold War. W. clues: Al Gore and the Florida recount, September 11, Dick Cheney, No Child Left Behind, Hurricane Katrina, and the 2003 Iraq War. If you hear “43rd,” “Texas governor,” or “Laura,” say “George W. Bush.”
trap.line: Real answer line: George Walker Bush (accept Bush 43 or Dubya; prompt on Bush or George Bush; do not accept or prompt on “George H. W. Bush” or “Jeb Bush”)

topics.name: Great Depression
topics.kicker: The economic collapse of the 1930s · Began with the 1929 stock market crash
topics.briefing: The Great Depression began when the New York stock market crashed in October 1929. Over the next few years, thousands of banks failed, and by 1933 about one in four American workers had no job. Families who lost their homes built shantytowns nicknamed “Hoovervilles,” after President Herbert Hoover, while dust storms drove farmers off the Great Plains, and the hard times lasted through the 1930s.
topics.answerHtml: Great Depression (prompt on Depression; do not accept “Great Recession” or “New Deal”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz blamed this crisis on the Federal Reserve, arguing in _A Monetary History of the United States_ that the Fed let the money supply shrink by about a third. In 2002, Ben Bernanke admitted the Fed’s role in this crisis, telling Friedman and Schwartz, “We did it. We’re very sorry.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economic disaster of the 1930s that followed the stock market crash of 1929.

tossups.p: More than a thousand economists signed a petition asking the president to veto a 1930 law that raised taxes on imported goods, but he signed it anyway. Other countries struck back with their own tariffs, and world trade shrank during this crisis.
tossups.r: That law was the Smoot–Hawley Tariff. For 10 points, name this economic crisis that began while Herbert Hoover was president.

tossups.p: Troops led by Douglas MacArthur drove thousands of World War I veterans out of their camp at Anacostia [“an-uh-KOSS-tee-uh”] Flats during this crisis. Those veterans, called the Bonus Army, had marched to Washington in 1932 to demand early payment of bonuses that were not due until 1945.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economic crisis of the 1930s, when millions of Americans lost their jobs.

tossups.p: During this period, people called old newspapers used as bedding “Hoover blankets” and turned their empty pockets inside out as “Hoover flags.” Cars pulled by horses or mules because their owners could not afford gasoline were mocked as “Hoover wagons.”
tossups.r: Shantytowns of the homeless were called Hoovervilles. For 10 points, name this economic crisis that followed the 1929 stock market crash.

tossups.p: Florence Owens Thompson was the subject of a 1936 photograph taken at a camp for pea pickers in Nipomo [“nih-POH-moh”], California, during this crisis. That photograph, Dorothea Lange’s _Migrant Mother_, shows a worried woman with her children.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economic crisis of the 1930s that Franklin Roosevelt fought with the New Deal.

tossups.p: On April 14, 1935, a day remembered as “Black Sunday,” a giant dust storm rolled across the southern Great Plains during this period. Years of drought and over-plowing had turned parts of Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas into the Dust Bowl.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economic crisis of the 1930s that began with a stock market crash.

tossups.p: Karen Hesse’s Newbery Medal–winning novel _Out of the Dust_, written in free verse, follows an Oklahoma girl named Billie Jo during this period. An earlier novel set during this period follows the Joad family as they drive west on Route 66 to California.
tossups.r: That novel is John Steinbeck’s _The Grapes of Wrath_. For 10 points, name this economic crisis of the 1930s.

tossups.p: In Christopher Paul Curtis’s novel _Bud, Not Buddy_, a ten-year-old orphan in Michigan searches for the man he believes is his father during this period. The musical _Annie_ is also set during this period, and in one song, people living in a shantytown sing “We’d Like to Thank You, Herbert Hoover.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this time of mass unemployment that followed the stock market crash of 1929.

tossups.p: The failure of Austria’s largest bank, the Creditanstalt [“kreh-DEET-ahn-shtahlt”], in 1931 helped spread this crisis across Europe. Later that year, Britain abandoned the gold standard, and in Germany the hard times of this crisis helped the Nazi Party win votes.
tossups.r: In the United States, Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal tried to end it. For 10 points, name this worldwide economic collapse of the 1930s.

tossups.p: Yip Harburg wrote the words to “Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?,” a 1932 song in which a man who had built a railroad and fought in a war ends up standing in line, waiting for bread, during this period.
tossups.r: Soup kitchens and breadlines fed hungry people across the country during this crisis. For 10 points, name this economic disaster of the 1930s.

tossups.p: In 1932, the president created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to lend money to banks and railroads during this crisis. That president, who had praised “rugged individualism” in his 1928 campaign, lost the 1932 election in a landslide.
tossups.r: That president was Herbert Hoover. For 10 points, name this economic crisis that began during his term.

tossups.p: Many investors had bought stocks “on margin,” using borrowed money, in the years before this crisis. Between 1929 and 1932, the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost almost 90 percent of its value, and it did not climb back to its 1929 peak until 1954.
tossups.r: At its worst, about one in four American workers had no job. For 10 points, name this economic disaster that Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal fought.

tossups.p: John Maynard Keynes [“KAYNZ”] argued in his 1936 book _The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money_ that governments should spend more to fight slumps like this one. Thousands of American banks failed during this crisis, wiping out many families’ savings before federal deposit insurance existed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economic disaster of the 1930s, which began with the stock market crash of 1929.

tossups.p: Writer James Agee [“AY-jee”] and photographer Walker Evans spent the summer of 1936 with poor sharecropping families in Alabama, a project that became the book _Let Us Now Praise Famous Men_. Government photographers such as Dorothea Lange also recorded the hardships of this period.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this time of economic hardship in the 1930s, when about a quarter of American workers had no job.

tossups.p: During this period, Midwestern farmers organized “penny auctions,” bidding only pennies when a neighbor’s farm property was auctioned off to pay debts, then handing it back to its owner. Milo Reno’s Farmers’ Holiday Association urged farmers to stop sending crops to market until prices rose.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this economic crisis of the 1930s, which began with the 1929 stock market crash.

The Dust Bowl: drought and dust storms drove farm families off the southern Great Plains

Troops under Douglas MacArthur drove the Bonus Army from its camp at Anacostia Flats
“Hoover blankets” (old newspapers), “Hoover flags” (empty pockets), and “Hoover wagons” (cars pulled by horses or mules)
Hoover, who praised “rugged individualism,” created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) to lend to banks and railroads

Florence Owens Thompson was photographed for _Migrant Mother_ at a pea pickers’ camp in Nipomo, California

Keynes’s _General Theory_ (1936) argued that governments should spend more to fight slumps

Set during it: _Bud, Not Buddy_ (Michigan), _Out of the Dust_ (Oklahoma, in free verse), and the musical _Annie_

trap.title: Depression, Recession, or Deal?
trap.body: Several answer lines sit right next to this one. The New Deal was Franklin Roosevelt’s set of programs to fight this crisis, the Dust Bowl was the drought and dust storms that hit the Great Plains at the same time, and the Great Recession was a different downturn that began in 2007. “Hoovervilles,” the shantytowns, can also be an answer of their own. Saying only “Depression” usually earns a prompt, so be ready to add “Great.”
trap.fix: Listen for the noun. “This crisis” or “this period” wants the Great Depression; “this program” or “these agencies” wants the New Deal; “this environmental disaster” or “these dust storms” wants the Dust Bowl; “these shantytowns” wants Hoovervilles. Clues about 2008, home mortgages, or TARP point to the Great Recession.
trap.line: Real answer line: Great Depression (prompt on Depression; do not accept “Great Recession” or “New Deal”)

topics.name: John F. Kennedy
topics.kicker: 35th U.S. President · Led the nation through the Cuban Missile Crisis
topics.briefing: John F. Kennedy survived the sinking of his torpedo boat, _PT-109_, in World War II and, at 43, became the youngest person ever elected president and the first Catholic president. In just under three years in office, he started the Peace Corps, set the goal of landing an American on the Moon, and steered the country through the Cuban Missile Crisis. He was assassinated in Dallas on November 22, 1963.
topics.answerHtml: John Fitzgerald Kennedy (or JFK; accept Jack Kennedy; prompt on Kennedy; do not accept “Robert F. Kennedy,” “Ted Kennedy,” or “John F. Kennedy Jr.”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After the Japanese destroyer _Amagiri_ rammed and sank this man’s patrol torpedo boat in 1943, he towed an injured crewman to an island by clenching the strap of the man’s life jacket in his teeth. He later kept a coconut shell, on which he had carved a rescue message, on his desk in the Oval Office.
tossups.r: That boat was _PT-109_. For 10 points, name this World War II hero who became the 35th president.

tossups.p: As a Harvard student, this man wrote a thesis about Britain’s slow preparation for World War II that became the book _Why England Slept_. He later won a Pulitzer Prize for a book about eight senators who risked their careers for their beliefs, including Sam Houston and Edmund Ross.
tossups.r: That book was _Profiles in Courage_. For 10 points, name this author who became the first Catholic president.

tossups.p: In 1960, this candidate won the West Virginia primary over Hubert Humphrey, and he told a group of Protestant ministers in Houston that he believed in an America “where the separation of church and state is absolute.”
tossups.r: That fall, he faced Richard Nixon in the first televised presidential debates. For 10 points, name this man who became the first Roman Catholic president.

tossups.p: During a 2 a.m. campaign stop at the University of Michigan in 1960, this man challenged students to serve their country by working overseas. As president, he created that program by executive order and named his brother-in-law Sargent Shriver its first director.
tossups.r: That program was the Peace Corps. For 10 points, name this president who said, “Ask not what your country can do for you.”

tossups.p: A plan drawn up under Dwight Eisenhower ended in failure less than three months into this president’s term, when about 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles of Brigade 2506 were defeated within days of landing in Cuba.
tossups.r: That invasion landed at the Bay of Pigs. For 10 points, name this president who later faced the Cuban Missile Crisis.

tossups.p: During thirteen tense days in October 1962, this president met with an advisory group called ExComm, whose members included his brother Robert. He rejected an air strike and instead ordered a naval “quarantine,” and the crisis ended when Nikita Khrushchev [“KROOSH-chef”] agreed to remove the weapons.
tossups.r: That standoff was the Cuban Missile Crisis. For 10 points, name this president who faced it.

tossups.p: In a June 1963 speech at American University, this president called for easing tensions with the Soviet Union. That summer, the United States signed the Limited Test Ban Treaty, which banned nuclear tests in the air, in space, and underwater.
tossups.r: Weeks after that speech, he told a crowd in West Berlin, “Ich bin ein Berliner.” For 10 points, name this president who was assassinated later that year.

tossups.p: Less than three weeks after Alan Shepard became the first American in space, this president asked Congress to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out. In a 1962 speech at Rice University, he declared, “We choose to go to the Moon.”
tossups.r: His goal was met in 1969, when Apollo 11 landed. For 10 points, name this president who started the Peace Corps.

tossups.p: At this president’s 1961 inauguration, sunlight glare kept Robert Frost from reading a new poem he had written for the day, so he recited “The Gift Outright” from memory instead. This president called his domestic program the “New Frontier.”
tossups.r: In his inaugural address, he urged, “Ask not what your country can do for you.” For 10 points, name this 35th president.

tossups.p: This president sent federal marshals and troops to the University of Mississippi in 1962 so that James Meredith could enroll as its first Black student. In a June 1963 television address, he called civil rights “a moral issue” and proposed a major civil rights bill.
tossups.r: That bill became the Civil Rights Act of 1964, signed by his successor, Lyndon B. Johnson. For 10 points, name this 35th president.

tossups.p: This man’s maternal grandfather, nicknamed “Honey Fitz,” served as mayor of Boston, and his father was the American ambassador to Britain when World War II began. His older brother Joseph Jr. was killed in that war while flying a dangerous mission as a Navy pilot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president whose younger brothers Robert and Ted also became U.S. senators.

tossups.p: In 1952, this congressman won a Senate seat in Massachusetts by defeating Henry Cabot Lodge Jr., who later ran for vice president against him. In 1956, he narrowly lost the Democratic nomination for vice president to Estes Kefauver [“KEE-faw-ver”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts senator who defeated Richard Nixon to win the presidency in 1960.

tossups.p: This president signed the Equal Pay Act of 1963 and created a commission on the status of women led by Eleanor Roosevelt. He also launched the Alliance for Progress, an aid program for Latin America.
tossups.r: He was assassinated in 1963. For 10 points, name this president who created the Peace Corps.

tossups.p: After this man’s death, his widow compared his time in the White House to “Camelot,” King Arthur’s court in a popular Broadway musical. New York’s Idlewild Airport and NASA’s launch center in Florida were renamed in his honor.
tossups.r: His face has appeared on the half-dollar coin since 1964. For 10 points, name this president who was assassinated in Dallas in 1963.

tossups.p: Federal judge Sarah T. Hughes swore in this man’s successor aboard Air Force One at Love Field, hours after this man was shot while riding in a motorcade through Dealey Plaza. This man is buried at Arlington National Cemetery, where an eternal flame marks his grave.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this president who was killed in Dallas on November 22, 1963.

trap.title: Which Kennedy?
trap.body: Real answer lines for this president prompt on just “Kennedy,” because several Kennedys show up in quiz bowl. His brother Robert F. Kennedy was his attorney general and later a senator from New York who ran for president in 1968, and his youngest brother, Ted Kennedy, served in the Senate for almost 47 years. Some questions ask for the whole Kennedy family, and questions about the 1963 assassination may want Lee Harvey Oswald or the event itself.
trap.fix: Only one Kennedy was president, so “this president” means John F. Kennedy; say the full name. RFK clues: attorney general, the 1968 campaign, and announcing Martin Luther King Jr.’s death in Indianapolis. Ted Kennedy clues: senator from Massachusetts from 1962 to 2009, a 1980 run against Jimmy Carter, and working with George W. Bush on No Child Left Behind.
trap.line: Real answer line: John Fitzgerald Kennedy (or JFK; accept Jack Kennedy; prompt on Kennedy; do not accept “Robert F. Kennedy,” “Ted Kennedy,” or “John F. Kennedy Jr.”)

topics.name: John Hancock
topics.kicker: President of the Continental Congress · Signed the Declaration in big letters
topics.briefing: John Hancock was one of the richest merchants in Boston, and in 1775 a British general offered to pardon every rebel who put down his weapons except him and Samuel Adams. As president of the Second Continental Congress, he was the first to sign the Declaration of Independence, writing his name so large that “John Hancock” became slang for a signature. He later served as the first governor of the state of Massachusetts.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1768, customs officials seized this merchant’s sloop _Liberty_, claiming he had unloaded Madeira wine without paying the tax on it, and a riot broke out in Boston. John Adams defended this man in court, and the charges were later dropped.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Boston merchant who signed the Declaration of Independence with a very large signature.

tossups.p: In June 1775, British general Thomas Gage offered a pardon to every rebel who laid down his arms except Samuel Adams and this man, whose offenses Gage called too serious to forgive.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot who was president of the Continental Congress when it adopted the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: When the Declaration of Independence was first printed in July 1776, only two names appeared on it: this man’s, and that of Charles Thomson, the Congress’s secretary. This man was serving as president of the Second Continental Congress at the time.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts patriot famous for his huge signature on the Declaration.

tossups.p: This man presided over the 1788 Massachusetts convention that debated the U.S. Constitution, and his proposal to recommend amendments helped win enough votes to ratify it. As governor, he also pardoned many of the farmers who had joined Shays’ Rebellion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first governor of the state of Massachusetts, who had signed the Declaration of Independence first.

tossups.p: After his father died, this boy was raised in Boston by his wealthy uncle Thomas, and in 1764 he inherited his uncle’s trading business, which made him one of the richest men in the colonies. He had graduated from Harvard in 1754.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this merchant who later became president of the Continental Congress and signed the Declaration of Independence first.

tossups.p: This man reportedly hoped to be named commander of the Continental Army, but John Adams nominated George Washington instead. A few weeks earlier, Congress had chosen this man to replace Peyton Randolph as its president.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Massachusetts delegate who later signed the Declaration of Independence in large letters.

tossups.p: In 1774, this man gave the yearly speech marking the anniversary of the Boston Massacre. Later that year, he was chosen president of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress, a Patriot government that met in defiance of the royal governor.
tossups.r: He later presided over the Second Continental Congress. For 10 points, name this patriot with a famously large signature.

tossups.p: On the night before the fighting at Lexington and Concord, this man and Samuel Adams were staying at the Lexington home of the minister Jonas Clarke. Paul Revere and William Dawes rode out from Boston to warn them that British regulars were on the march.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot who later signed the Declaration of Independence with a huge signature.

tossups.p: This man stepped down as governor in 1785, and James Bowdoin [“BOH-din”] was governor during Shays’ Rebellion before this man won the office back in 1787. He then held it until he died in 1793.
tossups.r: In 1780, he had become the first governor of the state of Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this Founding Father whose name became slang for a signature.

tossups.p: As president of Congress, this man signed George Washington’s commission as commander in chief of the Continental Army in June 1775. Three years later, he also signed the Articles of Confederation.
tossups.r: His bold signature stands out in the center of the Declaration of Independence. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts patriot and merchant.

tossups.p: After customs officials seized one of this merchant’s ships, the British turned it into a patrol ship, which angry colonists burned in Newport, Rhode Island, in 1769. That ship, the sloop _Liberty_, had been at the center of a riot in Boston the year before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this merchant who later became the first signer of the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: This man is buried in Boston’s Granary Burying Ground, near Samuel Adams, Paul Revere, and the victims of the Boston Massacre. In 1775, he married Dorothy Quincy. The Massachusetts State House was later built on land that had been this man’s cow pasture on Beacon Hill.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first governor of Massachusetts, whose large signature appears on the Declaration of Independence.

tossups.p: Samuel Adams helped this young merchant win a seat in the Massachusetts legislature in 1766, just after Boston traders boycotted British goods to protest the Stamp Act. The two men became leaders of the town’s resistance to British taxes.
tossups.r: In 1776, he signed the Declaration of Independence with a very large signature. For 10 points, name this president of the Continental Congress.

tossups.p: A Boston life insurance company founded in 1862 was named for this man, and skyscrapers in Boston and Chicago long carried his name. During his lifetime, his ships and his wharf in Boston made him one of the wealthiest men in New England.
tossups.r: His name became slang for a person’s signature. For 10 points, name this patriot who signed the Declaration of Independence first.

tossups.p: In 1785, Congress elected this man its president for a second time, but poor health kept him from serving. His first term as president had ended in 1777, when Henry Laurens [“LOR-unz”] of South Carolina replaced him.
tossups.r: A popular legend says he signed the Declaration of Independence in huge letters so that King George III could read it without spectacles. For 10 points, name this patriot.

His name became American slang for a person’s signature
President of the Second Continental Congress (1775–1777)
First governor of the state of Massachusetts (elected 1780)
One of the richest merchants in Boston and a leading Patriot
_Liberty_ affair (1768): customs officials seized his sloop _Liberty_, accusing him of smuggling, and a riot broke out
Paul Revere and William Dawes rode to Lexington to warn him and Samuel Adams (April 1775)

Reportedly hoped to command the Continental Army, but John Adams nominated George Washington
Signed Washington’s commission as commander in chief (1775) and the Articles of Confederation (1778)
Gave the 1774 Boston Massacre anniversary speech; president of the Massachusetts Provincial Congress
Stayed at minister Jonas Clarke’s house in Lexington on the night of Revere’s ride
Presided over the 1788 Massachusetts ratifying convention; his recommended amendments helped it approve the Constitution

trap.title: Two Hancocks, Two Adamses
trap.body: Winfield Scott Hancock was a different man: a Union general who held Cemetery Ridge at Gettysburg in 1863 and lost the 1880 presidential election to James Garfield. Clues about the night of Paul Revere’s ride name both this man and Samuel Adams, so players sometimes blurt out “Samuel Adams” instead, and John Adams, his lawyer in the _Liberty_ case, can be a trap too.
trap.fix: Revolution-era clues (the _Liberty_, the Continental Congress, the Declaration, the Massachusetts governorship) mean John Hancock; Civil War clues mean Winfield Scott Hancock. When a clue names two Patriot leaders, listen for which one the question wants: the rich merchant with the big signature is Hancock, and the organizer of the Sons of Liberty is Samuel Adams.
